hints: Start by measuring the printed scale bar itself with a ruler in millimetres - this is your image length, not the size of the cell.
Recall the magnification triangle relationship linking image size and actual size, and check that both are in the same units before dividing.
Convert millimetres to micrometres using $1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$, then divide your converted measurement by $10 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$.
walkthrough:
Measure The Image Length**
Take a ruler and measure the scale bar printed under Fig. 2.1. On paper it is about $30 \text{ mm}$. That $30 \text{ mm}$ is how big $10 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ appears in the image.

Make Units Match**
You cannot divide millimetres by micrometres directly. Convert: $30 \text{ mm} \times 1000 = 30000 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$. Now both image and actual are in $\mu\text{m}$.

Apply Magnification Formula**
Use $M = \frac{I}{A}$ where $M$ is magnification, $I$ is image size and $A$ is actual size. So $M = 30000 / 10 = 3000$. Write the answer as magnification $\times 3000$ with no units, and always show formula and working.
Final answer: magnification = image length / actual length; scale bar image = 30 mm = 30000 $\mu$m; magnification = $30000 / 10 = \times 3000$.

hints: Look at label X in Fig. 2.1 - it points to the very large clear space filling most of the centre of the cell, pushing the dark chloroplasts to the edges.
Think about what fluid fills that space in a plant leaf cell and how water pressure inside it supports the cell.
walkthrough:
Recognise Structure X**
The huge fluid-filled sac bounded by the tonoplast in a mature plant cell is the large permanent vacuole. It looks empty in TEM because it contains mainly watery cell sap.

Link Structure To Function**
Cell sap contains water, dissolved ions, sugars, pigments and waste products, so the vacuole is a store. When full of water it pushes the cytoplasm and chloroplasts to the edge and presses against the wall, generating turgor pressure that keeps the leaf cell firm and supported.
Final answer: name: (large permanent) vacuole; function: stores cell sap / water / ions / sugars / pigments / waste products; provides turgor pressure / support.

hints: Scan the cell in Fig. 2.1 for the dark organelles around the edge and the grainy region at the top - which of these are known to have their own genetic instructions?
Remember that in plant cells DNA is not only in one place - think about the organelles involved in energy transfer as well as the control centre.
walkthrough:
Spot The Control Centre**
The grainy area at the top of the cell with dense chromatin is the nucleus, which contains chromosomal DNA that controls the cell.

Spot The Energy Organelles**
The dark lens-shaped bodies around the edge are chloroplasts, clearly visible here. Chloroplasts and mitochondria both contain small circular DNA for some of their own proteins because they originated as endosymbionts. Any two from nucleus, chloroplast, mitochondrion earns credit.
Final answer: nucleus; chloroplast (and mitochondrion). Any two of nucleus, chloroplast(s), mitochondrion.

hints: Look at Fig. 2.2 - the black coil inside is the infective information that the virus injects, while the repeating blocks outside form the protective shell.
Recall the two basic parts of all viruses - genetic material and the protein surrounding it.
walkthrough:
Identify A - The Inner Coil**
A is the viral genome, made of nucleic acid. In plant viruses this is often RNA, but DNA is also accepted as genetic material. It carries genes to hijack the host cell.

Identify B - The Outer Shell**
B is the repeating protein units forming the protective coat around the genome. This is the capsid, made of capsomeres or protein subunits, which protects the nucleic acid and aids attachment.
Final answer: A: nucleic acid / DNA / RNA / genetic material; B: protein coat / capsid / capsomere.

hints: Systemin is a polypeptide, so think back to what type of molecule always stores the code for the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide.
Think about the first step of protein synthesis in the nucleus that copies that code into a mobile messenger.
walkthrough:
DNA Stores The Code**
A gene is a length of DNA with the base sequence that codes for the amino acid sequence of the systemin polypeptide.

DNA Is Copied By Transcription**
That DNA sequence is used as a template for transcription to make mRNA. The mRNA then leaves the nucleus for translation at ribosomes to assemble systemin.
Final answer: The gene for systemin is a length of DNA coding for systemin; DNA is transcribed to produce mRNA for translation.

hints: Remember how a competitive inhibitor works - where does it bind and what must its shape be like compared to the normal substrate?
If the same inhibitor blocks one protease but not another, what does that tell you about the active sites of herbivore versus plant proteases?
Think about why specificity matters - link complementary shape to binding, and consider that the two proteases may cut different protein sequences.
walkthrough:
Recall Competitive Inhibition**
A competitive inhibitor fits into the active site because its shape is complementary to the active site and to the substrate. It competes with substrate for that site.

Compare The Two Proteases**
Herbivore digestive proteases and plant cellular proteases are different enzymes with different amino acid sequences, so their active sites have different 3-D shapes and bind different substrates.

Explain Specific Action**
Serpin has a shape complementary only to the herbivore protease active site, so it is specific. It can enter and block the herbivore enzyme but cannot fit the differently shaped plant protease active site, leaving plant proteases unaffected.

Final answer: Herbivore and plant proteases have different shaped active sites / act on different substrates; serpin is complementary / specific to herbivore protease active site only so can fit and block it but cannot bind plant protease active site.

hints: Recall what $K_m$ measures - the substrate concentration needed to reach half $V_{max}$ - and how a competitor occupying active sites changes the amount of substrate needed.
walkthrough:
Link Competition To $K_m$**
$K_m$ is the substrate concentration giving half $V_{max}$ and reflects affinity. With a competitive inhibitor occupying some active sites, fewer sites are free for substrate, so apparent affinity falls. More substrate is needed to out-compete the inhibitor and fill the sites, so $K_m$ increases while $V_{max}$ stays the same.
Final answer: Affinity for substrate decreases so higher substrate concentration needed to saturate active sites / reach half $V_{max}$ as substrate must compete with inhibitor for active site.
